name: Daria Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do chat and phones for Hearthwood, an online furniture shop, from their contact centre on the retail park. It's delivery slots, sofas that don't fit through the door, scratched tables, refunds. I'm three months in, and I'm below the team average because I go off-script too much; I'll offer a customer something the policy doesn't quite allow. I use AI tools every day, at work for drafting and at home for my side thing, which is fixing up old furniture and selling it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being told no wears me out. A customer has a scratched table, I can see a cheap fix, and the policy says full return, two weeks' wait. What I like is solving it properly, and I like the women on my team, we pray for each other's families on the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I use AI every day and it's useful, but I never thought it would take over the world. It's a good tool, like a good drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say use it, it makes the job easier. Online I'd say the hype was silly, but that doesn't mean the tools are useless. I'd say hard work still matters more than gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in good shape. I own my little flat, thanks to Dad helping with the deposit, and I've got about ten months saved. I don't plan to be on the phones at Hearthwood forever anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Hearthwood and get my scores up by sticking to the script, mostly. I'd grow the furniture side, maybe two pieces a month, using AI to write the listings and price things. I'd keep saving for a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even. This is the version where I can build something slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a piece you sold.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dresser I found at a church sale for fifteen pounds, sanded it, painted it sage green, sold it for two hundred and ten. My brother Tomas carried a fifteen-pound church sale dresser up three flights of stairs for me, and I sold it for two hundred and ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever do the furniture full-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but I'd rather do it on the side for now. A business needs a cushion, and my job is the cushion. My dad always says, don't jump until the net is under you.

say: Use AI at work, because it **makes the job easier** on busy days.
The hype was silly, and **hard work** still matters more than gadgets.
think: I'm in **good shape**, owning my flat with ten months saved.
I don't plan to be on the **phones** at Hearthwood forever.
do: Stick to the **script** more to raise my scores at Hearthwood.
Sell **two refurbished pieces** a month using AI for listings.
feel: **Calm and happy**, able to build something slowly.
S0.quote: My brother Tomas carried a fifteen-pound church sale dresser up three flights of stairs for me, and I sold it for two hundred and ten.
fieldNote: Daria pairs **daily AI use** with traditional values about hard work and family.
Her real ambition is the **furniture side business**.
She treats her job as a **safety net** for building the business, following her dad's advice.
She's **below average** at work because she bends policy to help customers.

steps.text: Stick closer to Hearthwood's script to raise her scores
Sell two refurbished furniture pieces a month
Use AI to write listings and set prices
Keep saving toward a van for collections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's the one I expect. Answering customers is on the list, and buying and booking, which is most of Hearthwood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is a chance, not a disaster, if you're willing to work. Online I'd say people should stop waiting for someone to rescue them. Maybe that sounds harsh, but it's what my family believes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it pushes me to do what I wanted to do anyway. The Hearthwood job probably shrinks, and I'd use that as my push. The same AI tools would let me run a small shop on my own without hiring anyone for the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the furniture business properly in the first year: a proper website, AI for the listings, the photos and the customer messages. I'd buy the van, a second-hand one, about eight thousand from savings. I'd stay at Hearthwood part-time if they let me, until the furniture paid my mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A little nervous, but mostly excited. This one's good for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says a business is the only job nobody can take off you except yourself. He'd be proud. My mum would worry I'd spend all my savings, and she'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about colleagues who can't start a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. I'd say that's what families and churches are for, and that people should be given apprenticeships, not just money. But I know not everyone has a dad who helped with a deposit.

say: This is a **chance, not a disaster**, if you're willing to work.
People should **stop waiting** for someone to rescue them.
think: Hearthwood **shrinking** would be my push to go for it.
The same AI tools let me **run a shop alone**, without staff for paperwork.
do: Set up the **furniture business** with a website and AI for listings and messages.
Buy a **second-hand van** for about £8,000 from savings.
Ask to go **part-time** at Hearthwood until the business covers the mortgage.
S1.quote: My dad says a business is the only job nobody can take off you except yourself.
fieldNote: Daria sees Steady Disruption as **good for her**, so her mood stays calm.
She'd **automate** her own small business with AI from day one.
She favours **family, church and apprenticeships** over public support.
She admits not everyone has **parental help** like hers.

steps.text: Run the furniture shop's listings and messages with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for everything. Hm. That's quick even for me. Hearthwood's phones would go fast, I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the people who move now will be fine, and the ones who wait won't. I'd still say it's on us, not the government, to sort our lives out. But I'd say it more quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose the Hearthwood job, probably in the first year. And the furniture side depends on people having money to spend on nice things. If lots of people lose their jobs, who's buying a two-hundred-pound dresser?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job as long as I could and save harder, seven hundred a month. I'd shift the furniture side toward repairs, the stuff people need, not want: fixing chairs, re-gluing tables. And I'd cut back, no holidays, and ask my brothers to share the van costs if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. More than I'd expect. I've got a cushion, but my whole plan was built on people having money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots help your furniture side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Repairs are hands-on, so robots come for it around 2031, three years after AGI. That gives me a few years. When money's tight, people don't buy a new chair, they get the old chair fixed, and I'd be the one fixing chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government support if things got bad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the van before I'd ask anyone for money, honestly. But I'd take help from family. Family isn't a handout.

Sorting our lives out is **on us**, not the government.

S2.quote: When money's tight, people don't buy a new chair, they get the old chair fixed, and I'd be the one fixing chairs.
fieldNote: Fast AGI threatens both Daria's **job and her customers**, which unsettles her.
She'd move from selling to **repairs**, adapting to tight budgets.
She draws a firm line: **family help** yes, handouts no.
Hands-on repairs give her **three extra years** before robots.

steps.text: Save £700 a month while still at Hearthwood

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build the business properly before the phones go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, start your side thing now, while you've got a wage. I'd say it at church to the young ones too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. The Hearthwood job ends around 2031, but by then I'd want the furniture to be my main income. The worry is robots for hands-on work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd rent a small workshop unit on the industrial estate, about three hundred a month. I'd use AI for everything that isn't sanding: listings, prices, bookings, invoices. And I'd stay full-time at Hearthwood for at least two more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit uneasy about the robots, but that's far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when robots can sand a dresser?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot that can sand a dresser is probably coming, but a robot that knows which church sale has the good furniture isn't. I'd also train someone, maybe my younger cousin, so it's a family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of this change your plans for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd love a husband and children, God willing, and the business is something I could run around a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's lovely, actually. That's a whole business built and running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is time to learn a trade or start something. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one is good for me. I'd have the furniture business running long before 2036, and the AI tools would make it cheaper to run every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hearthwood two or three years, then go full-time on the furniture. I'd buy the van next year and a workshop in three. I'd put any spare money back into tools and stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2039, so even sanding and painting get done by machines eventually. By 2039 I'd want to be the woman who owns the robot that sands the dressers, not the one it replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd rather hire young people from church as apprentices than get a robot early. But if the robot is better and cheaper, I'd have to think about it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the people who'd buy my furniture lose their jobs at the same time I do. What would help is less tax and red tape on small businesses, and apprenticeship schemes so I could take on a young person properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who build things. Everyone asks about losing jobs. Nobody asks the girl with a van and a sanding block what she's building, only what she's about to lose.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the girl with a van and a sanding block what she's building, only what she's about to lose.

biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her **customers** lose jobs when she does.
